d.title: Four problems, four answers, and the third is the one people underrate
d.caption: **An RNN compresses everything it has read into one fixed-size vector, so information about token 5 must survive being overwritten 500 times to reach token 505. Attention has no such compression — token 505 reads token 5 directly.** That is a different claim from the gradient one: even with perfect optimisation, the bottleneck is a capacity limit rather than a training difficulty. And the last row is why the architecture won in practice: **the whole computation is matrix multiplies.**

state: a direct connection between any two

d.title: Attention is faster up to 256 tokens and slower at 512
d.caption: The crossover is the measurement worth having, because the usual summary is that attention is the fast one. **It is 1.84× faster at 32 tokens, and 0.75× — slower — at 512.** Which is exactly what the complexity says: **attention is `O(n²)` in sequence length and an LSTM is `O(n)`, so parallelism wins at short lengths and the quadratic term wins eventually.** The transformer's advantage at scale is **hardware utilisation and gradient paths, not asymptotic cost.**

d.title: The feed-forward network is twice the attention block
d.caption: At the paper's configuration, **attention is four 512×512 projections for 1,050,624 parameters and the FFN is 512→2048→512 for 2,099,712 — so the FFN is 2.00× the attention block.** Which is the opposite of where the attention goes when the architecture is explained: **two thirds of every encoder block's parameters are in the part with no interaction between positions at all.** 4.6 is about what that part does, and 4.10 counts the whole model this way.

d.title: Attention cannot tell “the cat sat” from “sat cat the”
d.caption: 4.3 shows attention is **permutation-equivariant** — shuffle the input rows and the output rows shuffle identically — so **the mechanism genuinely cannot distinguish one word order from another.** Since order carries most of the meaning in language, **position has to enter somewhere, and the transformer adds it to the input embedding** rather than building it into the mechanism. Which is a design choice with consequences: **it is the only place order lives, so every variant in 4.9 is a variant of this one addition.**

nodes.label: So: add it to the input embedding
Which is why 4.9 has so many variants

d.title: Each pair of dimensions is one frequency, as sine and cosine
d.caption: **At position 0 every sine is 0 and every cosine is 1, which is why the first row alternates `[0, 1, 0, 1, ...]`** — the position-0 encoding is not a zero vector. The structure is the point: **dimensions `(2i, 2i+1)` hold the sine and cosine of the *same* frequency, and that pairing is what makes the rotation property in §05 possible.** Every value lies in [−1, 1] by construction, so the encoding cannot blow up at any position.

d.title: Wavelengths from 6.28 positions to 60,611
d.caption: The frequencies are a **geometric** range, so the wavelengths span four orders of magnitude: **dimension pair 0 completes a cycle every 6.28 positions, and pair 255 every 60,611.** Which is what gives the encoding its resolution at both ends — **the fast dimensions distinguish adjacent positions, and the slow ones distinguish regions of the sequence** — and why the longest wavelength being far longer than any sequence you train on matters: that dimension is effectively a linear ramp.

d.title: Unique, equal-norm, and smoothly decaying — all three checked
d.caption: **Max off-diagonal cosine over 200 positions is 0.973055, so no two positions collide.** Every position vector has norm exactly **16.0000** — `sqrt(d_model/2)` — **so no position is intrinsically louder than another**, which matters because the encoding is *added* to the embedding. And the dot product decays smoothly with separation: **0.9731 at k=1 down to 0.3374 at k=199. That last property is the useful one: attention scores can pick up distance directly from the encoding.**

d.title: Three starting positions, one offset, and the rotation predicts all three exactly
d.caption: The paper's stated motivation is that **`PE[pos+k]` is a linear function of `PE[pos]` for any fixed offset `k`** — and within one frequency pair that linear function is **a plane rotation by `ω·k`.** Checked at three different starting positions with `k = 7`, the prediction matches to four decimal places every time. **Which is why the sine/cosine pairing of §02 is load-bearing: a rotation needs two components, and the encoding supplies exactly two per frequency.**

d.title: The stated justification is backwards: embeddings were already larger
d.caption: The reference multiplies the token embedding by `sqrt(d_model)` **because otherwise the positional encoding would dominate.** Measured with `nn.Embedding`'s default `N(0,1)` init: **token RMS 0.9963 against PE RMS 0.7071 — the embeddings are already 1.41× larger.** After multiplying by `sqrt(512) = 22.6274` the ratio is **31.88**, so the scaling does not prevent domination, **it makes the positional signal 32 times quieter than the token signal.** Which may still be the right thing — **and it is not the stated reason.**

d.title: Five steps hide in one line, and three of them are just a projection
d.caption: **Query — *what am I looking for?* Key — *what do I contain?* Value — *what do I deliver?*** All three are the same input through a different learned matrix, which is why the mechanism is symmetric in shape and asymmetric in role. Then `QKᵀ` makes an `(n × n)` score matrix where **entry (i, j) is how much position i should attend to position j**, the scale keeps it out of §04's saturation, and the softmax rows become the weights that average V.

nodes.label: Q = X W_Q: what I am looking for
K = X W_K: what I contain
V = X W_V: what I deliver
Scale, softmax each row, average V

d.title: The prediction is sqrt(d_k), and five measurements confirm it to three decimals
d.caption: If each component of `q` and `k` is independent with mean 0 and variance 1, then `Var(q·k) = d_k`, **so the raw scores have standard deviation `sqrt(d_k)` — which is a prediction, not an argument.** Measured over 200,000 random pairs per row it holds at every scale: **at `d_k = 1024` the measured variance is 1023.72 against a predicted 1024.** Which is why the `1/sqrt(d_k)` divisor is exactly the right constant rather than a tuned one.

steps.note: an exact constant, not a tuned one

d.title: The gradient peaks at a score std of 4 and collapses on both sides
d.caption: The cost of saturation is not that the distribution is peaked — **it is that the gradient dies.** Mean gradient norm rises from 4.11e−2 at std 0.5 to **8.25e−2 at std 4.0 and falls to 3.16e−2 at std 16**, by which point one position holds 0.9016 of the mass and the entropy is 0.2521 against a possible 4.1589. **So an unscaled layer is not merely confident, it is hard to train.** The second measurement shows the fix working: **unscaled score std 8.1742 and entropy 0.3638, scaled 1.0218 and 2.9981.**

d.title: Everything is quadratic in n except the one step people worry about
d.caption: Read the memory column rather than the time column. **`QKᵀ` materialises an `(n × n)` matrix and so does the softmax, so memory is `O(n²)` regardless of `d` — which is why a long sequence runs out of memory before it runs out of time, and why FlashAttention's contribution is not computing the score matrix faster but never storing it.** And the final `weights · V` step is `O(n² d_v)` in time but only `O(n·d_v)` in memory, because the output is the same shape as the input.
